name: attributes a single-entry/fixed-size capacity to singletonMap vs characterizes it only by immutability
side_a: No_deduct when the answer attributes a size/capacity property to the singletonMap — any wording that says it holds one entry or is fixed-size for a single entry ('contains exactly one entry', 'fixed-size map designed for a single entry'), including as a contrast with HashMap's ability to hold multiple entries.
side_b: Deduct when the only property the answer ascribes to singletonMap is immutability/read-only-ness (and to HashMap, mutability), with no statement of how many entries it holds — e.g. 'singletonMap creates an immutable map, while HashMap allows modifications' — even though the name 'singletonMap' is used.

name: Ties the wrapping to this code's actual call site (messageParams) vs gives only a generic textbook rationale
side_a: no_deduct — the answer explains why THIS code wraps the singletonMap, naming the actual consumer (the `messageParams` method) and hypothesizing that it needs/expects a mutable map.

name: Requirement attributed to the specific messageParams parameter vs. stated generically (unnamed APIs / no callee named at all)
side_a: Award credit when the answer ties the HashMap requirement to the actual receiving method/parameter (messageParams), i.e., names the callee whose parameter is declared as HashMap.
side_b: Deduct when the answer explains HashMap-vs-singletonMap only in the abstract — no mention of messageParams, or only a generic reference to 'APIs that expect ...' / 'the code uses HashMap' — since the sub-item is about the declared parameter of that specific call, not a general property of maps.

name: Asserts the parameter requirement vs. offers it as one speculative possibility among alternatives
side_a: Award credit when the answer asserts, without hedging into alternatives, that the parameter is/must be a HashMap.
side_b: Deduct when the HashMap-parameter claim is presented only as a guessed option in a disjunction ('likely ... either requires a mutable map ... or specifically expects a HashMap type'), because the answer does not commit to the declared parameter type as the reason.

name: Definite finding that the code never alters the map vs. speculative guess that mutability might be needed
side_a: Do not deduct when the answer makes a definite, asserted claim about the actual behavior of the code — that the map is in fact not altered / not written to after being handed to messageParams — even if that claim is tacked on as a concession and no call sites are named. A flat statement of fact about the real usage ('the map isn't altered later') satisfies the sub-item.
side_b: Deduct when the answer only offers hedged conjecture about why a mutable map might be wanted ('likely because the method modifies the map or expects a mutable implementation', 'can later be modified ... or be passed to APIs that expect a mutable HashMap'), without ever committing to a finding about what messageParams actually does. Speculation framed as possible reasons leaves the read/write question unresolved and biases toward mutation, so it does not count as noting the usages are read-only.
